stimulus.text:
Population of the United States, counted by the federal census:

| Year | Population |
| --- | --- |
| 1800 | 5,308,483 |
| 1820 | 9,638,453 |
| 1840 | 17,069,453 |

Miles of railroad track in operation: 23 miles in 1830 and 2,818 miles in 1840.

Source: United States census counts, 1800–1840; National Bureau of Economic Research, Business Annals, railroad mileage.
stimulus.source_note: Population from United States census counts, 1800-1840; railroad mileage from National Bureau of Economic Research, Business Annals (23 miles in 1830; 2,818 miles in 1840).

source: original; data from United States census counts and National Bureau of Economic Research, Business Annals
stem: According to the tables, about how many times larger was the population in 1840 than in 1800?

options.misconception: Two times 5.3 million is about 10.6 million, well short of 17 million.
Ten times 5.3 million is about 53 million, far above 17 million.
The population more than tripled, so it was far from the same size.

rationales.A: Divide 17 million by 5.3 million. The answer is about 3.2, so about three times larger is right.
rationales.B: Two times 5.3 million is 10.6 million. The 1840 count of 17 million is much larger than that.
rationales.C: Ten times 5.3 million is 53 million. The 1840 count of 17 million is much smaller than that.
rationales.D: The table shows 5.3 million in 1800 and 17 million in 1840. The population grew, so it was not the same size.
rationales.general:
1. Read the two numbers. The census counted about 5.3 million people in 1800 and about 17.1 million in 1840.
2. Divide to compare. Seventeen divided by five is about three, with a little left over.
3. Name the size of the change. A country that triples in forty years is growing fast.
Remember: to compare two counts, divide the later one by the earlier one.
